title: Mesopotamia
objective: After this level you can describe Mesopotamian art, from stepped temples to carved seals.
summary: Mesopotamian cities raised stepped mud-brick ziggurats, like Ur's for the moon god Nanna, and carved tiny stone cylinder seals that printed pictures on clay.

cards.headline: The first cities built their temples out of mud.
cards.body: Mesopotamia is Greek for "between rivers": the land of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the world's earliest civilization grew up. Its builders worked in brick, and its artists often worked in something humbler still: clay. This level runs from a temple tower down to a picture about the size of your thumb.

cards.headline: A staircase for a god
cards.body: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower. Picture a stack of ever-smaller brick platforms, like a giant wedding cake. The core was mud brick, wrapped in a tougher skin of baked brick. The best known, at Ur, went up about 2100 BCE under King Ur-Nammu for the moon god Nanna. Three staircases led up, and on the flat top sat a temple. The tower's whole job was to lift that temple up.

cards.fact: A cylinder seal prints a whole picture strip in one roll.
cards.context: Carve a design into a small stone cylinder, often no bigger than 5 cm tall, about the size of your thumb. Roll it across wet clay and the carving comes out raised, as one continuous band, the way a patterned paint roller works. Scholars count these tiny carvings among Mesopotamia's finest art.

cards.headline: A signature you could roll
cards.body: Seals weren't just decoration. Rolled onto clay, a seal marked what you owned or made a document legally binding: rolled on a tablet, it showed you had authorized the text, like a signature. Remember Level 1's writing, about 5,200 years ago? It was Sumerian cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into soft clay with a stylus. In Mesopotamia, words and pictures shared the same wet clay.

questions.explanation: A ziggurat was a stepped tower of mud brick and baked brick. Ur's, built about 2100 BCE for the moon god Nanna, had a temple on top.

questions.prompt: Why would a Mesopotamian roll a cylinder seal across a clay tablet?

options.label: To smooth the clay before writing
options.rationale: The seal left a raised picture, not a flat surface.

options.label: To count the days of the month
To show they had authorized the document
To glaze the tablet so it would last
options.rationale: The seal left a design; it didn't glaze anything.

questions.explanation: A seal's impression marked property or made a document legally binding, like a signature.

questions.prompt: Level 1 dated writing to about 5,200 years ago. What material did Sumerian writers and seal owners both use?

options.label: Papyrus scrolls
options.rationale: Sumerian writing was pressed into clay tablets.

options.label: Painted plaster walls
options.rationale: Seals and cuneiform both needed something soft to press into.

questions.explanation: Cuneiform was pressed into soft clay with a stylus, and seals were rolled across wet clay, often on the same tablet.
